title: Plate Tectonics
seo_title: Year 8 Science: Plate Tectonics Worksheets (Australian Curriculum)
standard_text: Explain how the theory of plate tectonics accounts for the formation of landforms and geological events, and describe the evidence for it (summary of the Australian Curriculum v9.0 Science content description).
meta_desc: Free Year 8 science worksheets on plate tectonics: Earth's layers, Gondwana and evidence for continental drift, plate boundaries, earthquakes and volcanoes, and how fast the Australian Plate moves. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Earth's surface is made of moving plates.
key_sub: Plates move a few centimetres a year; most earthquakes and volcanoes occur at their boundaries.
body_html:
How to think about it

Earth's crust and upper mantle are broken into plates that move slowly over the hotter mantle.

  • Layers: crust, mantle, outer core (liquid), inner core (solid).
  • Evidence: matching coastlines, Gondwana fossils such as Glossopteris, rock ages on the sea floor, GPS measurements.
  • Boundaries: convergent (mountains, trenches, volcanoes), divergent (ridges, new sea floor), transform (earthquakes along faults).
Example

Plates move apart at a mid-ocean ridge. Boundary?

moving apart

Answer: divergent

Example

7 cm per year for 1000 years?

7 × 1000 = 7000 cm

Answer: 70 m

Common mistakes

  • Thinking plates float on liquid magma (the mantle is mostly solid rock that flows very slowly).
  • Thinking continents move quickly.
  • Mixing up convergent boundaries (mountains, trenches) and divergent boundaries (new sea floor).

faq.q: Why does Australia have few volcanoes?
faq.a: Australia sits near the middle of the Indo-Australian Plate, far from the boundaries where most volcanoes and earthquakes happen.
A supercontinent that included Australia, Antarctica, South America, Africa and India. It began breaking up about 180 million years ago.

items.e: Crust → mantle → outer core → inner core.

items.q: Who first proposed continental drift in 1912?
items.e: His idea was not widely accepted until sea-floor evidence was found.

items.q: Why does Australia have fewer large earthquakes and volcanoes than New Zealand?
c: Australia is in the middle of a plate; New Zealand sits on a plate boundary.
items.e: Most earthquakes happen at boundaries.

items.q: Why do South America and Africa look like they fit together?
c: They are the same shape by chance only.
They are on the same plate today.
They were once joined and have moved apart.
People drew the maps that way.
items.e: Matching rocks and fossils support this.

items.q: What forms where an ocean plate sinks under another plate?
c: a deep ocean trench and often volcanoes
items.e: This is called subduction.

items.q: What forms at a mid-ocean ridge?

items.e: This is seafloor spreading.

items.q: Why couldn't Mesosaurus have swum across the Atlantic?
c: It was a small freshwater reptile that could not cross a salty ocean.
items.e: Its fossils support the idea that the continents were joined.

items.q: Amelia reads: “Deep trenches lie along the edges of the Pacific Ocean.” What is the best explanation?
c: Wind blew the fossils across the ocean.
Old seafloor sinks back into Earth where plates collide.
items.e: Plates carrying continents and seafloor move a few centimetres per year.

items.q: Do continents float on the ocean?
c: No. Continents are part of plates that move over the hot, slowly flowing mantle.
items.e: The mantle rock can flow very slowly.

items.q: What is the theory of plate tectonics?
c: Earth's crust and upper mantle are broken into large plates that move slowly.
Earth's crust is one solid piece.
items.e: Plates move a few centimetres a year.

items.q: Fossils of the plant Glossopteris are found in Australia, Antarctica, India and South America. What does this suggest?
c: The plant grew everywhere on Earth.
The fossils were moved by people.
items.e: This was key evidence for continental drift.

items.q: Tom reads: “Seafloor rock is youngest at mid-ocean ridges and older farther away.” What is the best explanation?
c: New seafloor forms at ridges and spreads outward as plates move apart.
Animals swam across the ocean carrying the rocks.
items.e: Plates carrying continents and seafloor move a few centimetres per year.

items.q: What are tectonic plates?
c: large pieces of Earth's outer layer (lithosphere) that slowly move
items.e: Continents and ocean floors ride on plates.

items.q: What was Gondwana?
c: a supercontinent that included Australia, Antarctica, South America, Africa and India
items.e: It broke apart over millions of years.

items.q: Why did many scientists reject Wegener's idea at first?
c: He could not explain what force moved the continents.
He said the Earth was flat.
items.e: Convection in the mantle was later suggested.

items.q: Which kind of plate boundary forms deep ocean trenches?
c: no boundary: it is far from any plate edge
items.e: Convergent: plates collide. Divergent: plates separate. Transform: plates slide past.

items.q: Which feature is most likely at a convergent boundary?
c: a flat desert in the middle of a plate
items.e: convergent (plates move together): deep ocean trenches.

items.q: Which kind of plate boundary forms the Alpine Fault in New Zealand?
c: no boundary: it is far from any plate edge
items.e: Convergent: plates collide. Divergent: plates separate. Transform: plates slide past.

items.q: Tom studies the East African Rift, where plates move apart. What kind of plate boundary is it?
items.e: At a divergent boundary, plates move apart.

items.q: Which feature is most likely at a transform boundary?
c: sudden earthquakes along a fault line
the Southern Alps of New Zealand pushing up
a flat desert in the middle of a plate
items.e: transform (plates slide past each other): sudden earthquakes along a fault line.

items.q: Priya observes: “A fence that was straight is now offset by 2 metres across a crack.” What is the best explanation?

An earthquake moved the ground along a fault.

A glacier once moved through the valley.
